altyazi.metin: The solar panels we see on rooftops, in
fields and across deserts...
all start with a handful of sand.
Today we'll follow one panel's journey,
step by step, from the quarry to the
power grid. You'll see which furnaces it
goes through, how pure it has to be, and
how it gets to the site.
Let's begin.
The journey begins in a quarry.
The heart of a panel is silicon.
Silicon makes up about twenty-eight
percent of Earth's crust; after oxygen,
it's the most abundant element.
But it's never found pure in nature.
It's locked tightly to oxygen inside
quartz, silicon dioxide.
And not just any quartz will do:
producers look for high-purity deposits
with very little iron or aluminum.
The rock is mined, crushed, washed and
screened. The first raw material is
ready.
The crushed quartz goes into a giant arc
furnace together with carbon sources
like coal, coke and wood chips.
Thick carbon electrodes hang into the
furnace, an electric arc forms between
them, and the temperature approaches two
thousand degrees. At this heat, carbon
tears the oxygen away from the quartz,
and it escapes as carbon monoxide.
What's left is molten silicon.
Tapped from the bottom of the furnace,
it's called metallurgical silicon, about
ninety-eight percent pure.
The process uses enormous amounts of
electricity. And while this silicon is
good enough for aluminum alloys...
for a solar cell, it's still far too
dirty.
The most common way to purify it is the
Siemens process. Metallurgical silicon
first reacts with hydrogen chloride and
becomes a liquid compound,
trichlorosilane. This liquid is
distilled again and again to strip out
foreign atoms. Then, inside bell-shaped
reactors, it flows over thin silicon
rods heated to around eleven hundred
degrees. Pure silicon deposits on the
rods layer by layer, and over days the
rods grow thick. The resulting
polysilicon has fewer than one foreign
atom in a million. The rods are broken
into chunks and sent on to the next
step.
Now it's time for the crystal.
Chunks of polysilicon are melted in a
quartz crucible, inside a furnace filled
with argon, at over fourteen hundred
degrees. A tiny amount of dopant is
added to the melt to set the cell's
electrical character.
Then a small seed crystal touches the
melt. The seed is rotated and pulled
upward very slowly.
First a thin neck is formed, which stops
defects from spreading through the
crystal. Then the diameter widens and
the body of the ingot starts to grow.
Silicon atoms line up, copying the
seed's pattern. Hours later, out comes
an ingot several meters long, made of
one single crystal.
The method is named after the Polish
scientist who discovered it:
Czochralski.
The round ingot is first trimmed at both
ends, then its sides are cut away to
make a square block.
Today's most common wafer sizes are one
hundred eighty-two and two hundred ten
millimeters. Next, steel wires coated
with diamond grit, thinner than a human
hair, slice the block into thousands of
pieces at once. Each slice, a wafer, is
about 0.15 millimeters thick, thin
enough to flex between your fingers.
Part of the silicon is lost as dust in
this cut, which is why manufacturers
keep racing toward thinner wires and
thinner wafers.
Turning a wafer into a cell takes
several precise steps.
First, the saw-damaged surface is etched
away and the surface is textured.
This creates microscopic pyramids, and
light bounces between them and stays
trapped inside. Next, dopant atoms are
diffused into the surface at high
temperature, forming a p-n junction.
This is what actually makes electricity:
a permanent electric field forms at the
boundary of two different layers.
A thin anti-reflective coating of
silicon nitride goes on top, and that's
what gives the cell its deep blue color.
Finally, silver paste is printed in fine
lines and fired. These lines are the
roads that collect the electricity.
Every cell is measured under light and
sorted by efficiency.
Today's mass-produced cells can turn
roughly a quarter of the sunlight that
hits them into electricity.
On the module line, cells are often cut
in half first; half-cells reduce losses.
Then they're soldered together with thin
copper ribbons to form strings.
The strings are laid between tempered
glass and protective films, and the back
is sealed with a tough backsheet.
Before lamination, the panel gets an
electroluminescence image, which reveals
even micro-cracks invisible to the eye.
A laminator then fuses all the layers
into one piece with heat and vacuum.
An aluminum frame is fitted, and a
junction box with bypass diodes is added
on the back. Finally, every panel is
tested under a split-second flash of
artificial sunlight and gets a label
showing its power.
Finished panels are stacked on pallets,
fitted with corner protectors and
tightly wrapped. A pallet usually holds
around thirty panels.
A forty-foot container fits more than
six hundred. The containers go to port
and cross the oceans by ship.
At the destination they clear customs,
are loaded onto trucks and head for the
plant site. Every pallet that arrives is
counted, checked, and inspected for
damaged panels.
On site, work starts long before the
panels arrive. First comes a ground
survey, to calculate how deep the piles
must go. Then steel piles are driven
into the ground in straight rows by
pile-driving machines.
A mounting structure is built on top.
Some systems are fixed-tilt; others are
trackers, single-axis systems that
follow the sun all day.
Panels are carried one by one, placed
and secured with clamps.
Then the wiring begins: panels are
connected in series to form strings,
strings to inverters, and inverters to
the substation. Finally, the whole
system is measured, tested and
commissioned for grid connection.
And at last, the sun rises.
When photons in the light hit the cell,
they knock electrons in the silicon
loose. The electric field of the p-n
junction pushes those electrons in one
direction; the silver lines collect
them, and direct current is born.
As panels are connected in series, the
voltage rises. The inverter constantly
searches for the operating point that
draws the most power from the panels,
and converts the direct current into the
alternating current the grid uses.
A transformer steps up the voltage, and
electricity flows through power lines to
homes, factories and cities.
At a solar plant, this conversion runs
nonstop, all day long.
A solar panel produces electricity for
twenty-five to thirty years without
burning any fuel. Many manufacturers
guarantee that a panel will keep most of
its power even after twenty-five years.
In sunny regions, a panel pays back the
energy used to make it within a few
years. At the end of its life, most of
its glass, aluminum and silicon can be
recycled. A journey that began with a
handful of sand becomes energy that
lights up cities. Follow Kozmos Lab for
more in our Energy Sources series!
